newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia troops search for hostages at third site.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia troops search for hostages at third site.

text.p: Cambodian troops searching for mines expert Christopher Howes set out on Wednesday for a third rendezvous site as officials expressed fears for the safety of the Briton and his Khmer Rouge escort.

Search leader Major General Khan Savoeun said he was worried the group may have run into problems as fighting was heard on Monday from Phnom Chan, the third of three possible meeting points arranged via a Khmer Rouge go-between.
The escort failed to show at two other meeting points in recent days.

Hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas could be on the trail of Howes, 37, and his Cambodian interpreter, Houn Hourth, who were abducted while conducting mine clearance operations for the Mines Advisory Group in Siem Reap on March 26, the general said.

"I am very worried about the hostages. If they are arrested again, they might be killed or put in a secret place," Khan Savoeun said, adding that he believed some media reports on the two men may have alerted the hardliners to the men's escape.
Last week, military officials said Howes and Houn Hourth had escaped from the hardline guerrilla base at Anlong Veng near the Thai border, but the two men have not been seen.
British officials in Siem Reap said they had no confirmation of the men's escape, but that they were hopeful of good news.

Khan Savoeun said he had expected the fugitives to reach government lines three or four days after the bid for freedom was launched following a meeting on November 19 between Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay, armed forces deputy chief of staff, and the Khmer Rouge go-between, named as Phan Phat.
He said troops had been sent to Phnom Chan early on Wednesday morning from two different positions.
He expected it would take them one day to reach the mountain, located on the fringes of hardline-controlled territory about 200 kilometers (125 miles) north of Phnom Penh.

"After they reach Phnom Chan, if they see nothing, I will order them to move back immediately because this is a dangerous area," he said, adding that soldiers remained at the two other meeting points in jungle hill country.
He said if the fugitives had run into hardliners on Phnom Chan and escaped, it could take 10 to 15 days to reach the government.

"Until now, I don't know where they are holding the hostages," the general said in reference to Howes, Houn Hourth and an estimated 140 dissident Khmer Rouge guerrillas who are said to have helped the two hostages escape from Anlong Veng.
"We can't use radio contact. If we tried that, maybe the secret would be out," he said.

The ranks of the Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 regime, have been decimated by thousands of defections in recent months, but a group of 800 to 2,000 hardliners are estimated to remain in the Anlong Veng area.
